title: So this will could be hated on but needs to be said. We should embrace AI tools in game development (at least for the small devs)
author: Braunb8888
selftext:
Here is why. I have absolutely no coding experience and even less of an idea of how to use unreal, godot etc, trust me I’ve tried.

But I’ve also been sitting on a 40 pages game design document I wrote for my masters degree 10+ years ago and it’s something I’ve been able to do absolutely fuck all with because unless you’re at a game company nobody gives a shit and even if you’re in one, getting that document pitched is a monumental effort in itself.

I’ve also got no budget to mention, so I can’t hire people to create this for me. That’s where AI tools come in. Over the past 2 nights I’ve been using Claude and godot to create my vision.

And it is my vision, down to the character designs which I fed into various programs to get usable playable versions out of, down to the dialogue, the style of font, the environments, that’s all me.

But without these new ai tools, that’s just all been a word document sitting on now 3 different computers.

I’ve been dying for a game like Xenogears or Valkyrie Profile to appear again and while some get close, most miss exactly what I’m looking for. That’s what my game will be like.

I’ve designed the combat system, edited attack animations for hours, etc, the work is real. 10 hours in so far and I’ve got most of act 1, with plenty more to go. That is the thing I’m trying to get across. Claude is a great assistant, but unless you have a vision that’s in depth and clear, it’s not going to be able to do shit with it.

So if you think this stuff is easy, I implore you, if you have a thought about a game that should be made, don’t be afraid to use these tools to make it. This is allowing people with a vision and a story but no technical skills to finally see their dream games come to fruition.

comments.author: ElderZombie250
comments.body:
I mean, anyone who is coding in any domain, who isn't using AI in some way, as a code reviewer or a brainstorming partner at the least, is kneecapping themselves.

Other areas remain controversial or even hated, such as AI generated assets, but for coding it's just pure foolishness not to use these tools.

I predict that in 12-18 months though, the backlash against AI will largely disappear because AI will be literally everywhere in our lives and being angry about it will be increasingly pointless.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
I paid for GitHub Copilot just for the autocomplete at first lol. It's a great increase in coding speed, taking out a lot of the manual stuff I had to do. 

It took me nearly a month to try out the Plan mode and plan out a feature in detail. After giving feedback on the plan and correcting it when I need to, things started changing. A good plan can be read and implemented by the AI, or by you. It can give estimadtes on how long parts of the plan will take if you code it by hand. 

I often just hand things to an agent to implement these days, but early on when I was doing most things by hand, plans were really valuable. I would have a fairly full picture about what I needed to write, and could do it myself.

replies.author: DonkeyBonked
replies.body:
I've made GDDs for my games and feature flow charts since my first dev team back in 2019. I won't make a game without one now.

Which goes hand in hand withe my first back story I wrote back in 2016 for a JRPG I made in RPG Maker, which is why I wouldn't make such a game without one again.

In my early days I just tried to keep it all in my head which often made scope creep way worse. Once you experience doing it the right way, it's really hard to go back to doing it the wrong way.

I've been making games since the 90s, and I blame scope creep and poor planning for why I wasn't more successful at it back then. That's why for like the first 20 years I made games, I only did it as a hobby. I even had a chance back then if I had been more disciplined, I could have worked at Interplay which I really wanted to.

Now, I'm much more methodical and have a very structured and systemic way to develop my games. I don't want AI taking over my creativity, but I don't mind the idea of AI tools empowering it. If your game is well structured and your GDD and flow charts are indexed with Copilot, autocomplete considers what you are doing with its suggestions.

It's not as "fast" as telling Claude "make me a complete game clone make no mistakes" 😂 but it's so much faster than writing it all by hand.

Sometimes it's right almost immediately and sometimes I have to get a little deeper into what I'm doing before it figures it out, but it's almost never that it doesn't speed things up and sometimes it thinks of stuff I forgot when I started the function.

Yes, I know autocomplete is technically AI, but I know everything it's writing is just what I'd be doing anyway and in the end I can own every single function in my code base.

My current game I prototyped and worked on for a long time before I discovered autocomplete, it would already be published if I had started with it. I love it and I don't feel uncomfortable at all like I don't know my own code. I read every function,  method, and confirm every class, and I have a very structured system for constants that autocomplete seems to work really well with.

I just write that code like 5x faster now, which is badass.

comments.author: Ciubowski
comments.body:
I think the bigger issue is polish. We all hear about it with big game developers and publishers that sometimes take longer to polish a game that is technically finished. They take months, maybe a whole year to fine tune stuff that is working but not working great.

And with AI we get this fake impression that even though it's capable of *doing it*, it's not capable of doing it right.

And as a result, we skip the "polish" phase more than often once we see the first results because.... hey! it's our game, it's made out of "nothing" after all. We didn't create everything by hand and somehow it's a working demo/prototype.

That amazes us at first and it makes it easy (very easy) to overlook the actual "costs" behind the scenes. The AI *did it* though, but maybe it did the first thing that was feasible and accepted our acceptance of that result.

Here's my example: I asked it to create me a hub for my main menu. And it did. But at what cost? Well basically it used the original 2D renderer which I thought was good enough to create 3D renders. *SOMEHOW* it did it instead of it pushing back and telling me "change the renderer" or "here's a better solution". Because it didn't push back. It just did what I asked.

And after trying to reduce random garbage in my animations, lighting and so on, I just asked it "what is the best way to do this?" and it just told me "changing the renderer and how we do the lighting".

I had no idea what I've missed. I was so blown away at the first version of my main menu that I totally skipped the "better solutions".

https://i.redd.it/dechch881pyh1.png

I've cut the time to calculate the Hub *in half* by doing per-corner lighting alone instead of the "one per pixel" version i had previously.

Of course a developer and graphical programmer would know this and probably even better solutions, but man... I've made my game more responsive on medium-to-low end tablets and devices.

Not to mention bringing my vision to life. That's the biggest thing.

This aside, I think the "majority" of vibe coders out there just accept the first solution and run with it, making their games look like a cheap pile of slop instead of iterating and asking the right questions out of the AI.

I took an internal training on "AI prompts" and I laughed it off thinking that "how hard is it to ask the AI questions?".

Turns out if you don't think your questions all the way through and mention everything that needs to be mentioned (also having a huge document on hand really helps) you'll be stitching your game piece by piece instead of doing it right from the get go.

Give the AI your whole doc (make it first if you haven't) because it definitely helps it having the full picture instead of starting from one irelevant element that you think it's the most important one.

comments.author: NebulaRisingGame
comments.body:
Only 10 hours in so far?  Unless this game is very simple.  Expect to spend 100s and 100s of hours with AI to get the game close to production ready.  Especially if you have zero software development experience, you will miss major areas.  But test, get claude to run security, automated testing, accessibility and best practice audits periodically against the code base.  

AI tools definitely make it possible for solo devs to do great things.  But expecting to build a quality production ready product quickly is very naive, as very evident with most games that are launched/posted here wayyyyyyy before they are ready.

comments.author: office-canard
comments.body:
Same here. I can't code either, and I've released 23 small games in about six months working with Claude. You're right that the vision is the part that can't be handed off. In the past I would have hired a musician, an illustrator and a coder and managed all of them. Now I give those jobs to AI, but deciding what the game is and judging whether it's fun is still entirely on me.



And along with the vision, there's the feel. Whether it feels good in your hands is something AI can never judge, and to me, feel is the most important thing in a game.



A Xenogears-style game is a big dream. Good luck with Act 2.
